content: Perineal trauma is a common occurrence during childbirth and is often associated with significant pain. Modern maternity care practices include various pain relief methods, one of which is the localized application of cooling treatments to the perineal area. This review aimed to assess the effectiveness of such cooling treatments compared to no treatment, placebo, or other cooling methods for alleviating pain caused by perineal trauma after childbirth. The review included 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,233 women. These trials compared different cooling treatments, such as ice packs, cold gel pads, and combinations of cooling with compression, to other cooling methods, placebo treatments, or no treatment. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was low or uncertain, but the inability to blind participants and personnel to treatment allocation introduced a high or unclear risk of bias in all trials. Cooling treatment (ice pack or cold gel pad) versus no treatment: Limited evidence of very low certainty suggested that cooling treatments might reduce self-reported perineal pain within 4 to 6 hours after childbirth (mean difference [MD] −4.46 on a 10-point scale; 95% confidence interval [CI] −5.07 to −3.85; 1 study, 100 participants). Pain reduction was also observed between 24 and 48 hours postpartum (risk ratio [RR] 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.94; 1 study, 316 participants). The evidence regarding wound healing, such as gaping wound edges five days postpartum, was very uncertain (RR 2.56; 95% CI 0.58 to 11.33; 1 study, 315 participants). Women’s satisfaction with perineal care was generally similar between those who received cooling treatments and those who did not. A minor reduction in psychospiritual comfort (MD −0.1 on a 5-point scale) was noted with cooling treatments, but this was not clinically significant. Cooling treatment (cold gel pad) with compression versus placebo (gel pad with compression): Low-certainty evidence indicated a trivial reduction in pain (MD −0.43 on a 10-point scale; 95% CI −0.73 to −0.13; 1 study, 250 participants) at 24 to 48 hours postpartum when cooling with compression was compared to placebo. Levels of perineal swelling (oedema) appeared similar between the two groups, and no perineal bruising was observed. Women in the cooling plus compression group rated their satisfaction with perineal care slightly higher (MD 0.88; 95% CI 0.38 to 1.38; 1 trial, 250 participants). Cooling treatment (ice pack) versus placebo (water pack): One study reported that no women in either group experienced pain within 24 hours postpartum. Low-certainty evidence suggested that perineal swelling was similar between the groups at 4 to 6 hours postpartum (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.50 to 1.86; 1 study, 63 participants) and within 24 hours postpartum (RR 0.36; 95% CI 0.08 to 1.59). No perineal bruising was observed in either group, and no adverse effects on wound healing were reported. Women’s satisfaction with the treatments was similar between the groups (RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.08; 63 participants), but the evidence was of very low certainty. Cooling treatment (ice pack) versus cooling treatment (cold gel pad): The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effects of ice packs versus cold gel pads on self-reported perineal pain, perineal bruising, or swelling at 4 to 6 hours or within 24 hours postpartum. Perineal swelling may persist 24 to 48 hours postpartum in women using ice packs (RR 1.69; 95% CI 1.03 to 2.7; 2 trials, 264 participants; very low certainty). The risk of gaping wound edges five days postpartum may be lower in women using ice packs (RR 0.22; 95% CI 0.05 to 1.01; 215 participants; very low certainty), but this effect did not persist to day 10 (RR 3.06; 95% CI 0.63 to 14.81; 214 participants). Women rated their satisfaction with ice packs less favorably five days postpartum (RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68; 1 study, 49 participants) and on day 10 (RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.73 to 0.92; 1 study, 208 participants), but the evidence was of very low certainty. Conclusions: There is limited and very low-certainty evidence supporting the use of cooling treatments, such as ice packs or cold gel pads, for relieving perineal pain in the first two days after childbirth. These treatments may need to be combined with other interventions, including pharmacological and non-pharmacological pain relief methods, to achieve adequate pain management. The studies reviewed involved cooling treatments applied for 10 to 20 minutes, and no adverse effects were reported. However, the small sample sizes and lack of high-certainty evidence warrant caution. Further well-designed trials are needed to establish the efficacy and safety of cooling treatments for perineal pain relief.
